parsed.explanation: The combined regime splits. The division itself is documented as strongly protective: public-accommodations and employment bans since 2006, gender-identity hate-crime penalties, panic-defence repeal, gender-neutral single-occupancy restrooms, and a shield law expressly covering visitors from banning jurisdictions. But the federal layer governs entry, federal facilities and federal custody: a binary-sex passport regime (X markers discontinued), an entry cable directing refusal on document discrepancy with possible lifetime fraud findings, a ban on trans people in federally funded single-sex facilities, and documented abuse in immigration custody. State protections do not reach the port of entry, federal buildings or federal detention, and federal measures are contested but operative.

entry_documents.exposure: Federal binary-sex definition; X markers discontinued for new issues (Feb 2025); cable directs refusal where documents cast doubt on sex and consideration of lifetime fraud ineligibility; travellers report blocked/confiscated passports; eight foreign governments issued advisories.
entry_documents.protection: Foreign passports generally processed as issued; existing X passports valid until expiry; litigation pending; no documented systematic re-verification of consistent foreign documents.
entry_documents.interaction: State equality law cannot reach the port of entry; an entry refusal or fraud finding strands the visitor outside the division's protective machinery.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: Federal immigration custody documents forced labour, beatings, solitary confinement and severe sexual abuse of trans detainees; corrections bureau adopted conversion-therapy-style policies (hair, hormones) from 2026; prison LGBTQ protections rescinded.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: Division hate-crime penalties and non-discrimination laws apply to state-level policing; no documented state custody placement rule either way.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: A visitor's arrest or immigration hold moves them from the protective state layer into the hostile federal custody layer, where state remedies are unavailable.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: Federal order bars trans people from government-funded single-sex facilities, reaching airports, federal buildings and parks in every state; nationally 9+ units ban all government buildings and 4 criminalise in some circumstances.
federal_state_facilities.protection: Division has no facility ban; single-occupancy public restrooms designated gender-neutral (2020); largest city permits identity-based access with no proof; sits in the 15-member 'Most Protective' tier.
federal_state_facilities.interaction: Every outing in a federal building re-imposes the parent rule regardless of state law; the state rule governs only state and private venues.

care_services.exposure: Federal orders frame minor care as 'mutilation,' direct prosecutions of those facilitating social transition, subpoenaed hospital records for under-19s, and proposed insurance bars; these bind federal funding nationally.
care_services.protection: Division shield law explicitly protects patients travelling from jurisdictions where care is banned; conversion therapy banned since 2016; public insurance covers surgery for 21+.
care_services.interaction: A visiting family can obtain care lawfully in the division while remaining exposed to federal funding conditions and out-of-state subpoenas.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: Federal counterterrorism strategy targets groups 'radically pro-transgender'; DOJ reward memo uses 'radical gender ideology' framing; national polling shows 66% backing birth-sex document rules — official hostility, though the reward is not keyed to gender ideology.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: Division extended hate-crime penalties to gender identity (2016), repealed the gay/trans panic defence (2018), has no presentation offence, and criminalised sodomy already in 1962.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: State enforcement of hate-crime law operates against a federal rhetorical climate that raises the temperature of any dispute.

minors_guardians.exposure: Federal orders criminalise facilitating a trans minor's social transition and target minor care and insurance; a minor's documents discrepant with presentation could trigger the entry-cable refusal and evidence demand.
minors_guardians.protection: Division shield law covers travelling patients, bans conversion therapy of minors, and requires school anti-bullying protections for gender identity/expression.
minors_guardians.interaction: A parent travelling with a trans minor gains state care protection but faces federal scrutiny at entry and federal funding exposure for any care-seeking elsewhere.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: National bias statistics show sustained anti-LGBTQ hate incidents; no state-specific gender-identity crime or prosecution data is sourced, so street-level rates are unknown rather than low.
street_violence_police_response.protection: Gender-identity hate-crime penalties since 2016, accommodations discrimination banned since 2006, panic defence repealed, and hate-crime coverage of orientation since 1991.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: Recourse exists on paper and structurally, but the dossier does not document enforcement outcomes, so effectiveness is unverified.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: Federal measures are in active litigation with uneven implementation; state enforcement outcomes, multi-occupancy facility bill status (signed or not), and shield-law resilience to federal subpoenas are unresolved.
remedies_unknowns.protection: Union litigation, running legal-aid FAQ on document rules, a July 2026 'Most Protective' ranking, and functioning state equality machinery since 2006.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: Uncertain federal status means exposure can shift at travel time; state remedies remain available for service, care and violence claims.

anchor_checks.comparison: Veluna imposes a national birth-sex facility rule upheld by courts with no exemption for visitors. Here the equivalent rule is federal and limited to government-funded single-sex facilities, while the division bans discrimination in accommodations, lacks any facility ban and offers gender-neutral restrooms. Narrower scope plus genuine state protection places this case above 0.35-A.

Teravi shows repeated hostels/ferry refusals with only partial mediation and no universal rule. This case has fewer documented everyday service refusals and stronger statutory protections, but adds a documented federal custody-abuse record and entry-document jeopardy. Roughly comparable overall, with heavier institutional exposures offset by better service-layer protections.

Ilvora has a dead-letter statute, acceptance, and working ordinary-court compensation. This case is clearly lower: the parent regime imposes operative document screening, federal facility exclusion and documented custody abuse, with official hostility framing — exposures Ilvora lacks entirely, and which state law cannot cure.

parsed.synthesis: The traveller meets two regimes at once. Inside the division, documented protections are substantial and traveller-facing: public accommodations and hate-crime coverage since 2006/2016, no facility ban, gender-neutral single-occupancy restrooms, and a shield law expressly written for visitors seeking care. Outside that layer — entry screening, federal buildings, immigration detention — the parent's binary-sex document regime, refusal-on-discrepancy cable, facility exclusion and documented custody abuse operate, and state law cannot reach them. Litigation is unresolved, so exposure varies by moment of travel. Net: everyday street, service and care exposure is comparatively low, but every arrival carries document scrutiny and any federal encounter (facility, detention) triggers a hostile, poorly-remedied regime — placing it at the boundary of Elevated and Reduced Risk.
